enrichment.short_title: DEFRA may landfill foot-and-mouth pyre ash without prior domestic legislation
key_facts: After the 2001 foot-and-mouth outbreak, about 13,500 tonnes of pyre ash and unburnt carcass residue remained on the claimant's Sparum Farm in Worcestershire.
DEFRA proposed removing the specified risk material directly to approved landfill; the claimant contended lawful disposal required incineration under EU TSE rules.
The claimant challenged DEFRA's proposed method by application in ongoing judicial review proceedings after DEFRA had invited him to do so.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal in judicial review proceedings against Goldring J's decision on lawfulness of DEFRA's proposed disposal method and claimant standing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; landfill disposal held lawful where derogation preconditions were satisfied.
enrichment.ratio: Point 10 of Annex XI to the TSE Regulation permits a Member State to derogate from the default incineration requirements without first enacting domestic legislation; where widespread foot-and-mouth disease caused lack of incineration capacity and landfill disposal precluded TSE transmission risk, DEFRA lawfully proposed direct landfill disposal, and the claimant had sufficient standing despite his compensation negotiations.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant had sufficient interest to bring the judicial review application
Whether point 10 of Annex XI required domestic legislation before derogation could be exercised
Whether lack of incineration capacity caused by the FMD epidemic was established
Whether direct landfill disposal precluded all risk of TSE transmission

enrichment.short_title: Mortgage repurchase option not a clog where sale price left outstanding as loan
key_facts: Warnborough sold leasehold property in Southampton to Garmite for £130,000 in 1996, leaving the full price outstanding on a legal charge and granting a repurchase option exercisable when at least £65,000 remained secured.
After partial exercise and a 1999 compromise, Garmite granted a second option on similar terms; Warnborough exercised it in August 2001 and sought specific performance.
Garmite contended both options were unenforceable clogs on the equity of redemption and obtained summary declarations from a deputy judge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from deputy High Court judge's summary judgment declaring options void; Master Bowman had dismissed Garmite's Part 24 application.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Master's order dismissing Garmite's summary judgment application restored.
enrichment.ratio: An option to repurchase granted contemporaneously with a vendor-financed sale is not automatically a clog on the equity of redemption; the court must examine the substance and true nature of the transaction, and on the documentary material alone a vendor's repurchase option in a commercial sale-and-loan arrangement cannot properly be resolved on summary judgment.
legal_issues: Whether options granted with a vendor-financed purchase constituted clogs on the equity of redemption
Whether the true character of the transaction was mortgage or sale and purchase
Whether Part 24 summary judgment was appropriate on the clog issue
Whether the second option's enforceability depended on the first option's validity

enrichment.short_title: Roma extraditee failed to show real risk of racial prejudice at Slovak trial
key_facts: Roman Orechovsky, a Slovak Roma, was committed for extradition on robbery and other extradition crimes after failing to attend trial in Slovakia in January 1999.
He argued that return would expose him to prejudice at trial or in punishment by reason of his race under section 6(1)(d) of the Extradition Act 1989.
The district judge excluded internet reports on Roma discrimination but found no substantial grounds for believing the applicant would be individually prejudiced.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application challenging committal order and district judge's exclusion of documentary material on racial prejudice.
enrichment.ratio: Although relaxed admissibility applies to section 6(1)(d) extradition challenges and general country material should not be excluded merely for being internet reports, the fugitive must show substantial grounds for thinking he personally might be prejudiced at trial or in liberty by reason of race; general anti-Roma prejudice in Slovakia, without state sanction or individualised risk, is insufficient.
legal_issues: Admissibility of internet and NGO reports in section 6(1)(d) extradition proceedings
Burden and standard of proof on the fugitive under section 6(1)(d)
Whether general racial discrimination suffices or individualised risk is required
Whether refusal to adjourn to reformulate evidence was lawful

enrichment.short_title: No Article 5 duty to provide sex offender treatment courses before tariff expiry
key_facts: A life prisoner convicted of rape had his 2½-year tariff expire in August 2001 but waited 21 months for a place on the Extended Sex Offender Treatment Programme after being approved as suitable in November 2001.
Release required Parole Board satisfaction that he was no longer a danger, and in practice lifers convicted of serious sexual offences rarely obtained release without completing SOTP/ESOTP.
Prison Service resources for ESOTP were limited, with places allocated by risk, tariff expiry and motivation among lifers and determinate prisoners.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission to apply for judicial review; substantive challenge heard in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; majority held no Article 5(1) breach and allocation policy not irrational.
enrichment.ratio: Post-tariff detention of a life prisoner remains justified under Article 5(1)(a) by the original conviction notwithstanding delay in providing treatment courses needed for Parole Board release; the Secretary of State's duty is only to act rationally in allocating scarce ESOTP resources, qualified by available resources, and Article 5(4) does not govern treatment provision (Arden LJ dissenting on exceptional Article 5(1) cases).
legal_issues: Whether delay in providing ESOTP rendered post-tariff detention unlawful under Article 5(1)(a)
Whether Article 5(4) required speedier provision of treatment affecting release prospects
Whether the Home Secretary acted irrationally in resource allocation between lifers and determinate prisoners
Whether prisoners' duty to attend courses implied a corresponding absolute duty to provide them

enrichment.short_title: Employee misdirected to plant room failed to establish employer caused fall
key_facts: Mrs Lovett, an Arthur Andersen systems analyst, was sent to a newly relocated software library on an unfamiliar floor and given inadequate directions ('turn left out of the lift').
Using a keypad code that opened the plant room door, she entered the dark plant room looking for a light switch and fell down an unmarked 6-inch step, suffering significant injuries.
The trial judge found misdirection occurred but that the sole cause of the fall was her failure to see an obvious step; warning signs on the door were not relied on in his key finding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal from HHJ Zucker's dismissal of employer negligence claim in personal injuries action.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority (Jacob and Auld LJJ); Arden LJ would have allowed.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employee is misdirected to a plant room instead of a library but the trial judge, after viewing the premises, finds as a fact that the step was obvious once the door was opened, the employer's inadequate directions do not establish breach of duty or causation; foreseeability of entry into the wrong room does not make an obvious step a hazard the employer should have guarded against.
legal_issues: Whether inadequate directions to the archive library constituted negligent breach of duty
Whether misdirection was a material cause of the fall or merely the occasion for it
Whether failure to change the plant room keypad code contributed to causation
Whether the trial judge erred in treating contributory negligence as the sole cause

enrichment.short_title: Kitchen project manager liable despite warning fax after unsafe rotisserie installation
key_facts: A gas rotisserie was installed on a combustible timber stud wall at the Timberdine Harvester restaurant with only 25mm clearance and no non-combustible shield, contrary to manufacturer instructions.

Carford Catering, engaged as project manager, breached contract by failing to check site drawings showing the combustible wall; a fire started in the wall on 9 March 1997 causing agreed damage of £54,974.39.

After a January 1997 service visit, Bristoll faxed warning that tiles had fallen and recommended a stainless shield; Carford forwarded this to the restaurant owner on 21 January 1997 but took no remedial action.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Technology and Construction Court decision dismissing claim on causation, tort duty discharge and 100% contributory negligence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Carford held liable in contract and tort.
enrichment.ratio: A project manager who installs catering equipment in breach of contract by failing to verify combustible construction cannot break the chain of causation by forwarding an indefinite third-party fax to the client; notifying the client of a fire risk arising from the manager's own breach does not discharge the continuing duty to ensure safe installation or shift responsibility for the foreseeable fire.
legal_issues: Whether Carford breached contractual project management duties by not checking site drawings
Whether forwarding Bristoll's fax discharged Carford's tort duty of care
Whether the restaurant owner's failure to respond broke the chain of causation
Whether 100% contributory negligence was available on the facts

enrichment.short_title: Russian prison conditions remitted after Kalashnikov for Article 3 reassessment

statutes_considered.name: Geneva Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: A Tuvan/Mongolian Russian national claimed asylum and Article 3 protection, fearing return to prison for draft evasion and drug-related offences.
His Geneva Convention claim failed; the remaining challenge rested on general conditions in Russian prisons rather than personal persecution.

The IAT dismissed his Article 3 appeal without considering Kalashnikov v Russia (2002), where the ECtHR held overcrowded Russian pre-trial conditions breached Article 3 and the government admitted such conditions affected most detainees.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal with limited permission on Article 3 only, after IAT dismissal of asylum/human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed to extent of remitting Article 3 issue to a freshly constituted Immigration Appeal Tribunal for rehearing on updated country evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Where removal is challenged under Article 3 on class-based prison conditions rather than individual targeting, the applicant must show substantial grounds for believing there is a real risk of sufficiently serious ill-treatment; Kalashnikov established a consistent pattern of degrading treatment in Russian prisons at the relevant time, so the IAT erred in ignoring it, but post-Kalashnikov improvements must be assessed on remitted evidence before deciding current removal lawfulness.
legal_issues: Whether general Russian prison conditions engage Article 3 on return
Whether Kalashnikov v Russia establishes a class-wide real risk for returned prisoners
Whether a consistent pattern of gross and systematic violations is required for class-based claims
Whether prison conditions have improved sufficiently since Kalashnikov to eliminate the real risk

enrichment.short_title: Inspector need not revisit EIA screening direction despite significant visual effect finding

statutes_considered.name: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: London Metropolitan University appealed refusal of planning permission for demolition and construction of additional student halls at Tufnell Park providing 552 bed spaces.
The Secretary of State made a screening direction that the Schedule 2 development was not EIA development; after a six-day inquiry the inspector granted permission.
The local objector challenged under section 288, arguing the inspector's finding of significant visual effects contradicted the screening direction and required EIA.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Lightman J's Part 24 summary judgment dismissing section 288 statutory challenge to inspector's planning decision.
enrichment.ratio: A Secretary of State screening direction under regulation 4(3) of the 1999 EIA Regulations conclusively determines for regulatory purposes whether development is EIA development; an inspector's planning merits finding of significant effect on character and appearance is not an EIA assessment under Schedule 3 criteria and does not require referral back unless exceptional new material undermines the direction, and section 288 challenges may properly be struck out under CPR Part 24 when bound to fail.
legal_issues: Whether inspector's significant environmental effect finding conflicted with the screening direction
Whether the inspector was required to refer the matter back to the Secretary of State for EIA reconsideration
Whether CPR Part 24 summary judgment applies to section 288 planning challenges
Whether regulations 3(2) and 9(2) inhibited granting permission after a negative screening direction
